analysis.one_liner: Raises the minimum wage with automatic future increases and protects striking workers from being permanently replaced.
analysis.headline: Wellstone's worker-security bill — a minimum wage increase, striker protections, and a cap on the tax break for executive pay — drew no cosponsors, never left the Senate labor committee, and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This omnibus bill bundled together many measures aimed at low- and middle-income workers. It would have raised the federal minimum wage to $4.70 and then $5.15 an hour and kept it rising automatically with average wages, banned companies from permanently replacing strikers, and stripped tax deductions from companies paying an executive more than 25 times their lowest-paid employee. It also would have made health insurance portable between jobs, required equal mental health coverage, consolidated federal job training into one-stop career centers, and set conditions for staying in NAFTA.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of minimum-wage workers would have seen their pay rise and then keep pace with average wages automatically instead of waiting for Congress to act. Union members would have gained leverage in strikes and first contract negotiations. Workers changing or losing jobs would have been able to keep health coverage without being denied for preexisting conditions, and people with mental health conditions would have gotten coverage equal to physical health benefits. Job seekers would have gotten coordinated one-stop career centers, and workers worried about trade would have gotten a renegotiated NAFTA with labor and environmental standards.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $4.70 an hour and then $5.15, and indexes it thereafter to a share of average hourly earnings so its value cannot quietly erode between congressional pay raises.
Makes it an illegal unfair labor practice for an employer to hire a permanent replacement for a striking worker or to deny a returning striker their job in favor of a replacement worker.
Denies employers a tax deduction for executive compensation above 25 times the lowest pay at the company, aimed at narrowing the gap between top and bottom pay.
Requires mediation and, if needed, binding arbitration when a newly certified union and employer cannot agree on a first contract.
Bars insurers from denying or refusing to renew coverage based on health status, limits preexisting-condition exclusions, and lets coverage carry over between jobs.
Requires mental health benefits to be treated on par with physical health benefits in limits and cost-sharing.
Consolidates many federal job training programs into an integrated system with one-stop career centers and public report cards on program performance.
Requires renegotiation of NAFTA — including raising labor, health, and environmental standards — and blocks its expansion unless specified conditions are certified as met.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum wages would bear higher payroll costs, and companies with very high executive pay would lose a tax deduction. Employers facing strikes would lose the ability to hire permanent replacements and would face binding arbitration in first-contract disputes. Health insurers would face guaranteed-issue and renewability rules limiting how they price and deny coverage. Companies relying on NAFTA as negotiated would face renegotiation of its terms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, especially low-wage and union-facing firms

drawbacks.text: The minimum wage increase would raise labor costs for small businesses and low-margin employers, and critics argued a sharply higher floor can reduce entry-level hiring.

The 25-times-lowest-pay deduction cap would be complicated to enforce and easy to restructure around, for example by shifting pay into stock or other forms not counted as salary, wages, or bonuses under the bill's definition.
Binding arbitration of first contracts takes final bargaining outcomes away from both sides and hands them to an outside arbitrator, which employers and some unions historically resisted.

The job training consolidation gave a new National Board power to block any workforce bill from floor consideration that it deemed noncompliant, a significant transfer of legislative control to an appointed body.

As an omnibus bill with nine titles spanning wages, tax law, labor law, health insurance, job training, pensions, and trade, it offered opponents many separate reasons to oppose it and no single provision likely to move on its own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions — a higher minimum wage that keeps its value, protection against permanent striker replacement, and portable health coverage — would have delivered real, direct gains to low-wage and working families, and Congress that same year did enact the same $5.15 wage level, showing the centerpiece was politically achievable. But the bill was deliberately sweeping: the executive-pay tax cap and the automatic wage indexation went well beyond what the 1996 Congress would accept, and the binding arbitration and procedural provisions drew plausible objections on the merits. Its zero cosponsors reflected breadth as much as opposition to any single idea.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to its labor committee the day it was introduced, nobody signed on as a cosponsor, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. Paul Wellstone introduced the Working Families Economic Security Act of 1996 in the Senate on May 2, 1996, with introductory remarks recorded in the Congressional Record.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, and no further action was ever taken on it.
No senator joined as a cosponsor; the cosponsor list shows zero.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any vote in either chamber, and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced a higher, automatically rising wage floor, companies facing union drives and strikes, and firms whose executive pay would have lost its tax deduction all came out ahead because the bill never advanced. Low-wage workers did get the same $5.15 minimum wage that year through a different, narrower bill, but without the automatic increases this bill proposed.

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor against a committee that never acted; the partisan shape of a floor fight was never tested.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (restaurants, retail, agriculture, other minimum-wage sectors)
industries.note: A $5.15 minimum wage plus automatic biennial increases tied to average wages would permanently raise their payroll costs, and indexing removes the periodic congressional pauses they historically relied on. Workers' gains come directly out of this cost avoidance.

industries.industry: Employers facing union organizing and strikes
industries.note: The bill makes permanent striker replacement an unfair labor practice and imposes binding arbitration on first contracts, removing two major sources of employer leverage in labor disputes.

industries.industry: Companies with very high executive pay
industries.note: Companies could no longer deduct executive compensation exceeding 25 times their lowest-paid employee's pay, raising the after-tax cost of extreme pay gaps.

Guaranteed issue and renewability rules and limits on preexisting-condition exclusions would restrict underwriting practices, but the bill keeps private plans as the channel for coverage, encourages medical savings accounts within HMOs, and relies on private purchasing cooperatives — leaving the industry's central role intact.

The bill repeals many existing training programs and folds their funding into a consolidated system with performance report cards and consumer reports; providers that perform well gain a clearer market, weaker ones lose their program silos.
